content: The use of Trecator (ethionamide) as a monotherapy for tuberculosis is strongly discouraged due to the rapid development of drug resistance. It is critical to administer ethionamide in combination with at least one or two other antituberculosis drugs to which the causative organism is known to be susceptible. The selection of companion drugs should be guided by susceptibility testing results. However, therapy may be initiated before the availability of susceptibility test results if deemed necessary by the physician. Commonly used companion drugs include rifampin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide, cycloserine, kanamycin, streptomycin, and isoniazid. The standard warnings, precautions, and dosage regimens for these companion drugs must be strictly followed. Patient adherence to the prescribed drug regimen is essential for the success of antituberculosis therapy and to prevent the emergence of drug-resistant organisms. Patients must complete the full course of treatment as prescribed. Directly observed therapy (DOT) is recommended to ensure compliance, particularly in patients receiving antituberculosis medications. In cases where drug-resistant organisms develop, consultation with experts in the treatment of drug-resistant tuberculosis is advised. Ethionamide may exacerbate the adverse effects of other antituberculosis drugs when used concurrently. Ophthalmologic examinations, including fundoscopy, should be performed prior to initiating therapy with Trecator and periodically during treatment. Patients should be instructed to report any occurrence of blurred vision or vision loss, with or without eye pain, during therapy. Excessive alcohol consumption should be avoided, as it has been associated with psychotic reactions. Baseline and monthly monitoring of serum transaminases (SGOT, SGPT) is recommended during therapy. If transaminase levels become elevated, ethionamide and any companion antituberculosis drugs should be temporarily discontinued until laboratory abnormalities resolve. The medications should then be reintroduced sequentially to identify the drug(s) responsible for hepatotoxicity. Blood glucose levels should also be monitored before and periodically during therapy, with diabetic patients being particularly vigilant for episodes of hypoglycemia. Thyroid function tests should be performed periodically, as hypothyroidism, with or without goiter, has been reported with ethionamide therapy. Trecator has been found to temporarily increase serum concentrations of isoniazid and may potentiate the adverse effects of other antituberculosis drugs. Convulsions have been reported when ethionamide is used in combination with cycloserine, necessitating special caution when both drugs are included in the treatment regimen. Excessive ethanol ingestion should be avoided due to the risk of psychotic reactions. Animal studies have demonstrated that Trecator has teratogenic potential in rabbits and rats at doses significantly higher than those recommended for humans. There are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women. Based on these findings, Trecator should not be used in pregnant women or those likely to become pregnant during therapy unless the prescribing physician determines it to be an essential component of treatment. The effects of Trecator on labor and delivery in pregnant women are unknown. There is no information available on the excretion of ethionamide in human milk. Therefore, Trecator should only be administered to nursing mothers if the potential benefits outweigh the risks. Breastfed infants of mothers taking Trecator should be monitored for adverse effects. Due to the rarity of drug-resistant pulmonary tuberculosis in neonates, infants, and children, investigations in these age groups have been limited. Trecator should not be used in pediatric patients under 12 years of age unless the causative organisms are definitively resistant to primary therapy and systemic dissemination of the disease or other life-threatening complications of tuberculosis are imminent.
